# Where the spoken words come from

The game says each word out loud. In drill mode the sound **is** the question —
the screen is a row of empty boxes — so a word we cannot pronounce is not a
degraded word, it is an unanswerable one.

This is the record of what we tried, what it cost, and what we settled on.

## Today: Kokoro-82M, generated by us

Every one of the 995 spine words has an mp3 in `data/audio/`, generated with
[Kokoro-82M](https://huggingface.co/hexgrad/Kokoro-82M) (Apache 2.0) on the GPU
box. Regenerate with `node tools/gen-audio.js`. Coverage is **995 of 995**, so
`playableSpine` is a safety net rather than a load-bearing trim.

**`data/audio/` is tracked.** That is the reversal that matters. The directory
used to be gitignored because it held Merriam-Webster recordings and their terms
forbid redistribution. The audio is now ours, so a fresh clone plays with sound
immediately: no API key, no `.env`, no ingest run, nothing to copy onto the
machine a child actually uses. ~14MB for the full list.

### How a word is rendered

Three decisions, each fixing a failure found by listening, not by reasoning.

**1. A carrier phrase: `Spell the word. ___.`**
Neural TTS is trained on sentences. Fed one bare word it clips the onset,
flattens the stress, or ends on a rising question intonation. The carrier fixes
all three, and it is how a spelling test is actually administered. It also gives
Whisper enough context to verify reliably — on a lone word Whisper is a language
model with nothing to condition on, and it hallucinates.

**2. Phonemes are pinned to the isolated rendering.**
Kokoro normalises text before phonemising it, and the carrier gives it context to
normalise *wrongly*: `Spell the word. am.` came out `ˌAˈɛm`, the letter names
A-M, the time abbreviation. Punctuation does not fix it — quotes, colon, comma
and dropping the period were all tried and all still said A.M.

So each word is rendered **alone** first, and that reading is pinned into the
carrier via misaki's `[word](/phonemes/)` override. A word in isolation has no
context to mislead the normaliser, which makes the carrier structurally
incapable of changing a pronunciation. No exception list: the next `am` fixes
itself.

**3. Reduced function words are promoted to citation form.**
English reduces function words nearly everywhere — "I'm", "she's" — so Kokoro
renders `is` as `ɪz`, `been` as `bˌɪn`: no primary stress, short and swallowed.
Correct for conversation, wrong when a child is asked to spell them. The rule: no
`ˈ` present → promote the `ˌ` if there is one, else put `ˈ` before the first
vowel. It fires on 64 of 995 words.

This matters more than the count suggests. The reduced words are very nearly the
same set M-W had no recording for — both are consequences of being high-frequency
function words — so the words most needing synthesis are the ones the model most
wants to swallow.

Rewording never fixes it: *"I think, therefore I am"*, sentence-final and
emphatic, still renders `æm`.

**The four exceptions.** Promotion adds the stress *mark*; it cannot restore a
*vowel*. A schwa does not record what the full vowel was, so `ə`/`ɐ` → `æ` is not
recoverable by any rule, and four words come out stressed and still reduced.
They are hand-written in `CITATION` in the remote `say.py`:

| word | forced | why |
|------|--------|-----|
| `a` | `ˈA` | the letter name, "ay" — "uh" is ambiguous to spell, and `a` is the first single-letter word in the spine |
| `an` | `ˈæn` | the way you say it when asked to spell it |
| `than` | `ðˈæn` | it rendered `ðˈən`, and Whisper heard **"then"** — itself a spine word |
| `the` | `ðˈi` | "thee" rather than "thuh"; both spell t-h-e, so preference, not correctness |

### Three audits that need no human ear

`tools/gen-audio.js` runs all three after every generation and refuses the run if
any fails. None is catchable by listening at this scale.

- **No drift.** What the carrier said, minus the carrier itself, must equal what
  was pinned. Catches the `am` → A.M. class of bug.
- **Nothing reduced.** Every pinned form must carry primary stress.
- **No stressed schwa.** `ˈə` or `ˈɐ` fails. This one exists because the previous
  check was not enough: `than` passed it as `ðˈən` and was still wrong. English
  never puts primary stress on a reduced vowel, so the combination is a reliable
  tell — and the failure it catches is invisible, because the audio sounds like a
  perfectly good recording of *a different word*.

A third check, Whisper round-tripping each file back to text, is available via
`speech-transcribe --expect` on the GPU box. It is weaker than it looks —
it **passed** the `am`/A.M. bug, transcribing "a.m." back to "am" — so treat it
as a homophone detector rather than a correctness check. Words it mis-spells are
words whose rival spelling a child could also type, which is the input to
`homophones.js` and the flash treatment.

## Yesterday: Merriam-Webster, and why we left

`tools/fetch-words.js` cached a pronunciation per word from the M-W Elementary
dictionary (`sd2`), falling through to Intermediate (`sd3`). It is kept as the
record of that path. **Nothing at play time calls it.**

It reached 597 of 634 fetched words. The 37 with an entry and no recording:

```
am are been brought came decided did divided does feet gave got had has held is
kept knew made men oh picked raised ran said sat saw seen stood these those
thought told took was went were
```

M-W files pronunciation on the base headword, so `sat` returns an entry that
cross-references `sit` and carries no audio of its own. `selectEntry`'s headword
guard refuses to file `sit`'s audio under `sat`, and that guard was correct —
playing "sit" to a child asked to spell "sat" is worse than silence, and it fails
*inaudibly*, because it still sounds like a working game.

That list is the whole argument. `is`, `was`, `said`, `had`, `did`, `got` are
among the most frequent words in English, and the game could not ask for any of
them. Four problems went away at once: the coverage gap, the API key and quota,
the redistribution ban, and a voice blended across many studio takes.

The recordings are preserved at `data/audio-mw/` — gitignored, because they are
still M-W's data — as the independent reference for checking our own. Where both
exist they should say the same word.

## Not chosen: browser `speechSynthesis`

Still the fallback when a file is missing, but it cannot be the plan. Measured in
Chrome 2026-08-02, foregrounded, after a browser restart:

```
voices: 199 (180 local, 19 remote)
speechSynthesis.speak(u)  ->  speaking: true, pending: true, NO start/error event
```

The queue wedges and stays wedged; `cancel()`, `resume()` and an explicit voice
all made no difference. `js/audio.js` therefore reports `'silent'` rather than
claiming a success it never observed, and the game warns after two silent words.

Two reasons not to lean on it even when healthy:

- **The default voice was `Karen`, en-AU.** We never select a voice, so the
  browser picks. Australian vowels differ exactly where English spelling is
  hardest — not cosmetic for a game whose entire task is mapping sound to letters.
- **19 of the voices are remote**, and using one means network egress during
  play, which the design forbids.

## Not chosen: macOS `say`

Available with no new dependency, and genuinely usable — `Samantha` is the only
en_US voice installed of 25. Rejected after A/B against both M-W and Kokoro: it
is clearly the most synthetic of the three, it is macOS-only, and it would tie
the word list to one platform's voice. Kept in mind only as an emergency path.
